abstract.p: Class imbalance remains a critical challenge in machine learning, as it often leads to biased predictions where algorithms disproportionately favor the majority class, resulting in the misclassification of minority class instances and reduced overall model performance. This study explores an innovative approach to addressing class imbalance in Random Forests by combining pruning with resampling techniques. While pruning typically improves performance and reduces computational costs, its effectiveness can be limited in complex ensembles dealing with imbalanced data. To tackle this, the proposed method incorporates three resampling strategies: under-sampling the majority class, over-sampling the minority class, and a hybrid of both. After balancing the training data, multiple trees are grown from bootstrap samples, and only those with low out-of-bag error rates are selected for the final ensemble. The classification performance of the proposed method is evaluated and compared against standard algorithms including k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN), Tree, Random Forest (RF), Balanced Random Forest (BRF), and Support Vector Machine (SVM). The results demonstrate that the proposed method outperformed its competitors in most of the cases.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Prediction accuracy of machine learning algorithms (MLA) is high when the observations in the dataset are evenly distributed between the two classes. The performance of MLAs is often jeopardized, however, when one class in the dataset has fewer observations (i.e., minority group) than the others (i.e., majority group). Such disparity in observational density, called the class-imbalanced problem1–3, is common in binary classification, where unequal number of class observations can lead to poor performance of the MLA. Class imbalance can lead to biased predictions, where the machine learning algorithm disproportionately favors the majority class, often misclassify instances of the minority class4,5. In such cases, the strong likelihood that the minority class might be underrepresented in the imbalanced data due to the fewer observations lead to a bias in the classification6. In particular, a high imbalance ratio (IR) makes it harder to classify because there are fewer examples in the minority class. Because of this, classifiers usually create decision boundaries with biased opinions toward the majority class. This makes it harder for the minority class to be recognized, and it gets worse as IR rises. Consequently, machine-based classification of imbalanced datasets is very difficult, particularly when dealing with massive or missing data sets and may require non-standard machine learning methods to achieve an adequate efficiency7. To enhance MLA’s performance for class imbalance data, different strategies including adjusting thresholds, over-sampling and under-sampling approaches, and cost-sensitive learning have been suggested8,9. Class-imbalance issue is particularly problematic in applications like fraud detection, medical diagnosis, and anomaly detection, where accurately identifying minority class instances is critical. To address the class-imbalance problem, various strategies such as data resampling techniques (over-sampling and under-sampling), algorithmic adjustments, and ensemble methods have been developed10,11. Despite these efforts, achieving high prediction accuracy while maintaining generalizability in imbalanced datasets remains a significant challenge in machine learning research12–14.

The MLA based classification of imbalance data is often divided into three categories4,15,16. First, there are data-level strategies that aim to achieve a balance between the observations in the two classes by randomly discarding some observations from the majority class (i.e., under-sampling the majority class) or by repeatedly using some observations from the minority class (i.e., over-sampling the minority class), or by combining both techniques. Second, algorithm-level strategies that alter weight of each observation during algorithm training or the output to minimize bias toward the majority class17. Third, a combination of both strategies (i.e., data-level and algorithm-level techniques) have also been proposed to improve the MLA-based classification performance of imbalanced data. Random Forest (RF) has been extensively studied for handling and classifying imbalanced data in a variety of predictive problems (see foe example,18–23. Several modifications to the RF algorithm have been proposed and implemented to efficiently handle the class imbalance problem24,25. For example, the weighed RF scheme, which is based on the concept of cost-sensitive learning, assigns a relatively larger weight to the training set of the minority class26. This strategy is shown to be more effective with classifiers derived from decision tree learning methods. Biased RF is another algorithm-level technique that can be combined with any ensemble method that increases the number of classifiers representing the minority class, thereby generating an ensemble biased toward the minority class to compensate its low presence in the dataset27,28. Likewise, the approach of balanced RF systematically under-sample the majority class during the generation of bootstrap samples. The primary advantages of this technique include high efficiency for large imbalanced data set and tolerance to noise29,30. Moreover, it has been suggested to systematically combine balanced and weighed RF to integrate the benefits of both algorithms. Under-Bagging is another hybrid RF algorithm for handling imbalanced data, which combines bagging and the under-sampling technique. The concept of Under-Bagging has been customized to varying degrees and implemented under the name of Quasi-Bagging31, Asymmetric Bagging32, and Roughly-Balanced Bagging33. Other modifications over Random Forest for imbalanced data can also be seen in14,34–38.

In this study, Random Forest (RF) is selected due to its well-established robustness in handling high-dimensional data and its intrinsic ability to provide feature importance, which is particularly advantageous for imbalanced classification problems. Although other machine learning techniques may offer certain benefits in specific contexts4,39, RF’s balance of simplicity, interpretability, and consistently strong performance across a broad range of tasks makes it a versatile and widely-used ensemble method. Additionally, RF’s use of out-of-bag (OOB) error estimation and its efficiency in processing large datasets further motivated our focus on enhancing this algorithm. Our proposed method builds on RF by introducing a novel pruning strategy with the combination of resampling techniques aimed at improving performance in class-imbalanced scenarios, significantly increasing computational efficiency without compromising accuracy.

The aim of this study is to extend the modification of RF unbiased towards improving the predictive performance for imbalanced datasets. After designing the proposed ensemble, it was implemented for the classification of 10 benchmark imbalanced datasets. The classification efficiency, assessed with error rate, is compared with those of standard MLA such as k-Nearest Neighbor (k-NN), Tree, RF, Balanced RF (BRF), and Support Vector Machine (SVM).

sec.title: Classification and regression tree (CART)
Random forest
sec.p:
Regression trees are used as the base classifier in bagging, and they are developed using bootstrap samples extracted from the training data. The outputs are then averaged to get a single estimate41. For classification tasks, trees are formed on bootstrap samples taken from the training data, and a decision regarding the predicted class is reached by majority vote42. The enhanced variant of Bagging is called Random Forest. The following are the key steps of the Random Forest algorithm:
Create a specific number of bootstrap samples using the data.
Build a classification/regression tree for every sample in the bootstrap. The tree is built so that a random sample of features, rather than all the features, are chosen at each node for splitting, and this process continues until it reaches the terminal nodes.
New observations are analyzed by the trees before they get to the terminal nodes. A majority vote is used to decide about the class of the new data. The Pseudo code of Random Forest is given in Algorithm 1.

sec.title: Over-sampling and under-sampling techniques
sec.p: Resampling is one of the most effective methods for addressing class imbalance, offering two primary approaches: oversampling and under-sampling.

sec.title: Over-sampling the minority class
sec.p: In oversampling, additional instances are generated for the minority class by reproducing existing observations. This process attempts to double the number of minority class instances, ensuring a more balanced class distribution13. The key advantage of oversampling is that it preserves all the original information in the dataset. However, reproducing extra training instances can significantly increase computational costs, particularly with large datasets, which may become burdensome for some machine learning models.

sec.title: Under-sampling the majority class
sec.p: On the other hand, under-sampling is applied when the majority class contains an excessively high number of observations. This approach reduces class imbalance by selectively removing instances from the majority class while retaining all minority class observations13. Typically, half of the majority class instances are discarded to achieve balance. While under-sampling is computationally efficient, it comes with a critical drawback: the removal of potentially informative instances. This loss of valuable data can negatively impact the performance and generalizability of the classifier.
Both methods are widely used, and their selection depends on the characteristics of the datasets and the computational resources available.

sec.title: Combination of over-sampling and under-sampling
sec.p: In some methods the combination of both over and under sampling are used and are called hybrid sampling techniques in order to establish more balanced data sets43,44. Hybrid sampling procedure almost always outperforms the individual sampling techniques by merging the qualities of each individual methods. Using this notion, we also use the hybrid resampling procedure to balance the training data set.

sec.title: Selection of diverse trees
sec.p: We opted for pruning based on out-of-bag (OOB) errors because it offers an unbiased estimate of classification performance using internal validation without requiring a separate test set. This is particularly beneficial in class-imbalanced scenarios where data availability is limited. OOB error captures each tree’s contribution to the ensemble’s overall performance, focusing on how well each tree generalizes to unseen data. This helps mitigate the common issue of overfitting to the majority class, a frequent problem in imbalanced datasets.

Unlike other pruning strategies based on tree depth, node purity, or cross-validation error, OOB error directly assesses each tree’s generalizability to unseen data, retaining only the most predictive trees. By focusing on OOB error, our method prioritizes trees that enhance performance across all classes, especially the minority class, rather than optimizing metrics that favor the majority class. This approach strikes a balance between maintaining model complexity to capture minority class patterns and reducing computational costs, resulting in a more robust ensemble suited for imbalanced datasets.

sec.title: Re-sampling to create balanced bootstrap samples
sec.p: Bootstrapping is a frequently used resampling method for handling the class imbalance problem and minimizing the differences between two classes. It is implemented to estimate extra-sample prediction error and evaluate uncertainty by drawing samples from the training data. A bootstrap sample is generated by drawing samples with replacement from the original data46. This approach ensures that every observation has an equal chance of being included in the sample, which can lead to some instances being selected multiple times while others are omitted. By generating multiple bootstrap samples, the method creates diverse subsets of the data, allowing for robust estimation of model performance and variability. The following three strategies were adopted for bootstrapping to balance the class distribution and improve model accuracy.

sec.title: Software and packages
sec.p: The classification algorithm was developed and executed in R (version 4.4.1), which is publicly available at https://www.r-project.org/. For the implementation of Tree algorithms, “part” R package is used48. Random Forest and Balanced Random Forest are executed using “randomForest” R package49. Moreover, the R package “e1071”is employed for implementing k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) and Support Vector Machine (SVM).

sec.title: Results
sec.p:
Overall, the cohort of ten benchmark imbalanced datasets (Table 1) is classified using various machine learning ensemble methods: the proposed ensemble with under-sampling, over-sampling, and a combination of both under and over-sampling, k-NN, SVM, Tree, RF and BRF. The efficiency of each of these classifiers is quantified with the corresponding error rate. The results given in Table 2 reveal that in the first scenario, the proposed method, Pruned Random Forest (PRF), is performing better than the other methods on most of the datasets. PRF gives the best results on 6 out of 10 datasets. This reduction in classification error rate shows that the performance of Random Forest can be improved by considering under-sampling the majority of class observations with tree selection while learning from imbalanced datasets. In the second scenario, the proposed method involves balancing the training data by over-sampling the minority class observations. The proposed method performed better than the other methods on 7 out the 10 datasets. It is also noted that the gain in prediction accuracy was improved in this scenario as compared to the previous one. This follows that over-sampling the minority class observation is better than under-sampling the majority class observations for the pruned ensemble while learning from imbalanced datasets. In the third variant of the method where under-sampling the majority class observations and over-sampling the minority class observations have been used simultaneously to balance the training data. The results show that the proposed method is performing better than the other on most of the datasets i.e., 8 out of the 10 datasets. The gain in accuracy here is the highest as compared to the previous two scenarios. To facilitate the comparison, normalized error rates are computed for each dataset and presented in 2. The normalized error rate is defined as the ratio of the error rate of a classifier for a given dataset to the maximum error rate within the same dataset. To exemplify, maximum error rate for classification of hepatitis dataset is observed for k-NN. To compute the normalized error rate for hepatitis dataset, error rates of all seven ensemble methods are divided by the error rate of k-NN.

Analysis of Fig. 2 reveals several interesting features for the classification efficiency of the benchmark datasets. There is no uniform trend in the error rate of classifying the datasets by all classifiers. A different error rate is observed for each classifier for each dataset, presumably due to the different nature of each dataset. For instance, the Hepatitis dataset is best classified by RF (i.e., minimum error rate) while worst efficiency is observed for k-NN (i.e., maximum error rate). Likewise, the error rate to classify the Haberman dataset is almost the same for all classifiers. The proposed algorithm of PRF in tandem with a combination of both under and over-sampling demonstrated a minimum error rate of classification for eight out of ten benchmark datasets, including Bands, MUSK, Oil-spill, Guide 3, Guide 1, Spambase, Phoneme and Thyroid.Fig. 2

The box and whisker plot has been exploited to analyze the overall distribution of the normalized error rates (i.e., the mean, median, range and other quantitative characteristics) of all the classifiers. Figure 3 summarizes the normalized error rates of classification for all algorithms in the form of box and whisker plot. It may be noted that the box and whisker plot is a very comprehensive graphical tool for quickly visualizing almost all statistical variables of the data. Additionally, the box and whisker plot can be used regardless of whether the data have a normal distribution or not. The upper, middle and lower lines of the box represent the values of upper quartile, median and lower quartile, respectively. The whiskers (i.e., the lines extending from each end of the box) correspond to the lower and upper range of the data50. For data following normal distribution, these five parameters are representative of percentiles P75, P50, P25, P0, and P100, respectively. The small hollow box within the box plot represents mean of the data.

To extend the comparison of the proposed method (i.e., PRF) with the other classifiers, the normalized error rates of each classifier for all ten benchmark datasets are grouped in one box and presented in Fig. 3. It is obvious that the mean and median normalized error rate for classification of the ten benchmark datasets is minimum for PRF with a combination of both under and over-sampling, followed by PRF with over-sampling and PRF with under-sampling. The relatively short size PRF box suggest that its classification performance is very consistent among all ten benchmark datasets, resulting in small dispersion in the normalized error rates. The PRF with all three scenarios (i.e., with over-sampling, with under-sampling and with a combination of both under- and over-sampling) reveal almost similar range of normalized error rates (indicated by size of the corresponding box). It is interesting to note that the classification efficiency of RF is the closest to that of the proposed PRF, both in term of the mean and median normalized error rates. Moreover, the classification performance of the SVM classifier is largely inconsistent across the ten benchmark datasets, as indicated by the largest box size in Fig. 3.Fig. 3

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study proposes a modified approach to address the class-unbalanced problem by using ensemble-based techniques. Specifically, it explores the effectiveness of pruning a tree forest and applying re-sampling methods to develop an improved version of Random Forest ensembles. The proposed ensemble method in tandem with over-sampling, under-sampling, and a combination of both under-sampling and over-samplings implemented to classify benchmark datasets. The predictive accuracy of the proposed method is evaluated and compared with other standard algorithms, including k -NN, Tree, RF, BRF, and SVM. The results show that the error rate of the ensemble technique (i.e., pruning Random Forest) to classify the benchmark datasets is significantly (p < 0.05) lower than all other techniques. Moreover, the proposed pruning method does lead to a significant reduction in training time by eliminating less predictive trees, which not only enhances the model’s performance, but also reduces the computational burden. By selecting trees with the lowest out-of-bag (OOB) error rates, the ensemble becomes more efficient, requiring fewer trees to achieve high accuracy, thus reducing the overall time and computational resources needed during training.

The proposed method addresses the limitations of existing hybrid ensemble methods like Biased Random Forests and Balanced Random Forests (BRF) by combining pruning with advanced resampling strategies. Biased Random Forests often lead to overfitting on minority classes due to disproportionate class weighting, while Balanced Random Forest can lose data diversity by repeatedly sampling equal-sized class subsets, which also increases computational costs. Our proposed method improves data utilization employing three resampling techniques, under-sampling, over-sampling, and a hybrid approach ensuring a balanced representation of both majority and minority classes without discarding valuable data. By pruning trees with low out-of-bag error rates, the proposed method reduces computational burden and improves performance, making it more efficient than traditional methods. Empirical results on 10 datasets show that PRF consistently outperforms BRF and other standard classifiers, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving classification accuracy and computational efficiency in complex and imbalanced settings.

This study has focused on Random Forests due to their robustness and ability to handle complex data structures. However, the integration of pruning with resampling techniques can be extended to other ensemble methods, such as Gradient Boosting Machines (GBM). Future research could adapt pruning criteria and resampling techniques to fit GBM’s boosting framework, enhancing its ability to manage class imbalance. Additionally, adaptive sampling methods that dynamically adjust based on class distributions could improve model performance by focusing on minority classes during training. Incorporating deep learning for feature extraction could also improve results by identifying complex data patterns, offering a deeper understanding of class boundaries when combined with ensemble pruning and resampling strategies.
